cues.text: A Difficult Marriage Well Borne
Born around 331 to a Christian family in Tagaste in North Africa, Monica was given in marriage while still young to Patricius, a pagan official of the town known for a violent temper.
She also had to live under the roof of a mother-in-law of similar disposition.
Monica bore this difficult household, we are told, not with resignation but with an active, patient virtue that in time won the genuine respect of her volatile husband.
He never once, in all their years together, is recorded to have raised a hand against her.
His neighbors marveled at this restraint, and Monica herself attributed it entirely to prayer and to the deliberate gentleness with which she answered every provocation.
Seventeen Years of Tears
Of the three children Monica bore, her eldest, Augustine , would become both her greatest joy and her longest sorrow.
He was a brilliant, ambitious young man who fell in with the heretical Manichaean sect, took a mistress, and fathered a son out of wedlock.
He showed every sign of a mind and heart drifting further from the faith his mother had tried to instill.
Monica's response, across nearly two decades, was neither despair nor the harsh rejection a lesser mother might have chosen, but an unrelenting campaign of prayer, tears, and patient counsel.
It was so persistent that a bishop she once consulted for advice is said to have told her simply: it is not possible that the son of so many tears should perish .
Following Her Son Across the Sea
When Augustine, without telling her, slipped away by ship to Rome to advance his career, Monica's grief did not turn to abandonment but to pursuit.
She followed him first to Rome and then to Milan, where providence had placed, as bishop of that city, a preacher of extraordinary eloquence named Ambrose .

It was under Ambrose's preaching, and under his mother's unrelenting prayer, that Augustine's long resistance finally began, in the famous garden scene he would later immortalize in his Confessions , to give way.
It was a conversion Monica had prayed for through more years and more tears than most mothers are ever asked to give.
A Prayer Answered at Last
Augustine was baptized by Ambrose at the Easter Vigil of 387, Monica present to witness what she would later say was the one thing left in this world she had ever truly wanted.
In the months that followed, mother and son shared a period of deep spiritual conversation at Ostia, awaiting a ship back to Africa.
Augustine records this scene of shared mystical contemplation with unforgettable tenderness in his Confessions .
For a brief moment, mother and son were united not merely in blood but in the very vision of God they had both, in their different ways, spent so long seeking.
Death at the Journey's End
Monica fell ill and died at Ostia before the ship could sail, in the autumn of 387, at fifty-six years old.
Asked by her sons whether she feared to die so far from her native Africa, she answered, Augustine tells us, that nothing is far from God.
She had no fear at all of where her body might be laid, for the Lord would know where to find her on the day of resurrection.
Legacy
Monica's own sanctity has always been inseparable, in the Church's memory, from the sanctity of the son whose conversion she prayed for so long to see.
And rightly so.

She teaches every parent, every spouse, every believer who has ever loved someone still far from God, that persistent, patient, unglamorous prayer — offered not for years but for decades if necessary — is never wasted.
She teaches, too, that God's timing, however painfully slow it may feel to a mother's heart, is never in the end too late.
